specAnchors.text: understand oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer and changes in oxidation number, and the application of these ideas to reactions of s- block and p- block elements
know that oxidising agents gain electrons and reducing agents lose electrons

primer.text: When electrons move, oxidation numbers move with them. This note links the electron transfer picture to the arithmetic of oxidation numbers, then names the two agents of every redox reaction: the oxidising agent that accepts electrons and falls, and the reducing agent that donates them and climbs.

modules.title: Electron transfer through oxidation numbers
modules.opening: Oxidation numbers turn electron transfer into arithmetic. This lesson follows nitrogen and bromine through the ammonia-bromine equation, watching one climb from -3 to 0 while the other falls from 0 to -1, and concludes who donated electrons to whom.
keyPoints: Oxidation and reduction can be demonstrated by changes in oxidation number during a reaction.
In 2NH3 + 3Br2 -> N2 + 6HBr, nitrogen rises from -3 in NH3 to 0 in N2.
A rising oxidation number means the species has been oxidised.
Bromine falls from 0 in Br2 to -1 in HBr, so bromine is reduced.
Nitrogen reduced bromine by donating electrons across the transfer.

low.restatement: Read the oxidation numbers before and after the reaction; the species whose number climbs is oxidised, the one that falls is reduced, and the electron flow runs from the climber to the faller.
low.analogy: Two bank accounts after a transfer: the balance that went up paid the money out (lost electrons), the balance that went down received it (gained electrons).
low.examPointer: Always write both states with signs - 'N goes -3 to 0' - before naming oxidised or reduced; the arithmetic earns the marks.

medium.restatement: Oxidation-number shifts quantify electron transfer: each unit rise equals one electron lost per atom, so nitrogen's 3-unit climb per atom pairs with bromine's 1-unit fall per atom, and the coefficients balance the ledger across the equation.
medium.analogy: A currency exchange where each nitrogen customer sells 3 coins and each bromine till takes exactly 1 - you need three bromine tills per nitrogen customer for the books to close.
medium.examPointer: Connect the ratio of oxidation-number changes to the equation's coefficients when asked why 3 Br2 appear per 2 NH3.

modules.title: The oxidising agent
modules.opening: Every redox reaction employs two agents. This lesson profiles the oxidising agent: the species that oxidises something else by taking its electrons, dropping its own oxidation number in the process.
keyPoints: An oxidising agent oxidises another species by pulling its electrons away.
The oxidising agent itself gains those electrons and is therefore reduced.
Because it is reduced, the oxidising agent's oxidation number decreases.
The worked diagram shows the agent accepting electrons during the reaction.
Spotting the faller in an equation identifies the oxidising agent instantly.

low.restatement: The oxidising agent is the electron acceptor: it takes electrons from its partner, oxidises that partner, and falls in oxidation number itself.
low.analogy: A pawnbroker takes valuables (electrons) from clients (the species oxidised); the broker's drawer fills up while the client walks out lighter.
low.examPointer: Do not call the oxidising agent 'oxidised' - it IS reduced while it DOES the oxidising; the two roles are the classic exam trap.

medium.restatement: The agent's reduction is the mechanical cause of the partner's oxidation: accepting electrons pulls them off the partner, so the agent's oxidation number decreases by the electrons it accepts.
medium.analogy: A vacuum cleaner (the agent) reduces the dust pile by sucking (accepting) particles off the carpet (the partner), which loses them and is thereby cleaned out.
medium.examPointer: When asked to identify the agent, quote its oxidation-number fall with both states - assertion without arithmetic scores poorly.

modules.title: The reducing agent and the worked pairing
modules.opening: The reducing agent is the mirror twin. This lesson profiles the species that donates electrons, climbing as its partner falls, and works the four-reaction example where the bold species Fe2+ wins the agent title.
keyPoints: A reducing agent reduces another species by handing electrons over to it.
The reducing agent itself is oxidised, losing or donating electrons.
Because it is oxidised, the reducing agent's oxidation number increases.
A valid redox reaction needs both an oxidising and a reducing agent present.
Some substances can play either role, depending on their partner and the conditions.

low.restatement: The reducing agent hands electrons over: its own number climbs as it is oxidised, and its partner's number falls as it is reduced - both agents must appear for the reaction to be redox.
low.analogy: A donor at a blood bank: the donor (reducing agent) leaves with less (oxidised), the patient (partner) gains (reduced), and a transfusion needs one of each.
low.examPointer: In multiple-choice agent items, compute the bold species' oxidation numbers first - in the worked set, Fe2+ falling +2 to 0 wins the oxidising-agent title while Mg rises as the reducing agent.

medium.restatement: Donation drives the partner's reduction, so the reducing agent climbs in oxidation number; dual-role species such as hydrogen peroxide pick their direction from the partner's strength and the reaction conditions.
medium.analogy: A freelancer who can invoice or pay depending on the counterparty - the same species oxidises or reduces according to whom it meets.
medium.examPointer: For dual-role items, never assert a fixed role - say the role depends on the partner and the conditions to secure the mark.

glossary.definition: The species that accepts electrons from its partner, oxidising the partner while being reduced itself.
The species that donates electrons to its partner, reducing the partner while being oxidised itself.
The movement of electrons from donor to acceptor that underlies every redox reaction.
